Content:
Consider the graph of [MATH: y=e^x] below. We will use this graph to compute [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} e^x \, .]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/10cb3b62b88394cd36f707559e61b7d5]

Content:
From the graph, we see that as [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 1,] the value of [MATH: y] approaches [MATH: e^1.] So
[MATH: \lim_{x\to 1} e^x = e^1 = e.]

Content:
The limit of the function at a point is equal to the value of the function at that point, and this is true for any point, not just [MATH: x=1.] If [MATH: c] is any real number, we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to c} e^x = e^c.]

Content:
In fact, all exponential functions have this property. For [MATH: a \gt 0] and any real number [MATH: c,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to c} a^x = a^c.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the graphs of [MATH: y = 2^x] and [MATH: y = 2^{-x}] shown below. We will use these graphs to compute the limits at infinity.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b74353297f24c384ed5e0930e8238b73]

Content:
Considering [MATH: y = 2^x] first, we note that as [MATH: x \to \infty,] the function increases without bound, and as [MATH: x \to -\infty,] the function approaches zero. So

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to \infty} 2^x = \infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to -\infty} 2^x =0.]

Content:
The same properties hold true for any exponential function [MATH: y=a^x] where [MATH: a \gt 1.]

Content:
Now consider the curve [MATH: y=2^{-x}.] We have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to \infty} 2^{-x} = 0\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to -\infty} 2^{-x} =\infty.]

Content:
Again, the same properties are true for any exponential function [MATH: y=a^{-x}] for [MATH: a \gt 1.]

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty} -3\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x.]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty} -3\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

[MATH: lim_(x → − ∞) − 3((1)/(2))^{x} = − 3 ⋅ lim_(x → − ∞)((1)/(2))^{x}]

Next, we recall the graph of [MATH: y = \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x.]

From the graph, we see that the function increases without bound as [MATH: x] decreases. Therefore,

[MATH: \lim_{x\to-\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x = \infty.]

However, the negative factor [MATH: -3] changes the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that

[MATH: -3\cdot \lim_{x\to-\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x = -\infty.]

sections.readable_text: Compute [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} -5 \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{1+x}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit as follows:

[MATH: lim_(x → ∞) − 5((1)/(3))^{1 + x}|= − 5lim_(x → ∞)((1)/(3))^{1 + x}; = − 5lim_(x → ∞)((1)/(3))^{1} ⋅ ((1)/(3))^{x}; = − 5lim_(x → ∞)(1)/(3) ⋅ ((1)/(3))^{x}; = − (5)/(3) ⋅ lim_(x → ∞)((1)/(3))^{x}]

Next, we recall the graph of [MATH: y = \left(\dfrac 1 3\right)^x.]

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as [MATH: x] increases. So

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = 0,]

and finally, we have

[MATH: -\dfrac{5}{3}\cdot \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = -\dfrac 5 3\cdot 0 = 0.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the graph of [MATH: y=e^x] below. We will use this graph to compute [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} e^x \, .]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/10cb3b62b88394cd36f707559e61b7d5]

Content:
From the graph, we see that as [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 1,] the value of [MATH: y] approaches [MATH: e^1.] So
[MATH: \lim_{x\to 1} e^x = e^1 = e.]

Content:
The limit of the function at a point is equal to the value of the function at that point, and this is true for any point, not just [MATH: x=1.] If [MATH: c] is any real number, we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to c} e^x = e^c.]

Content:
In fact, all exponential functions have this property. For [MATH: a \gt 0] and any real number [MATH: c,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to c} a^x = a^c.]

---

[MATH: lim_(x → 1)(3^{2x} + 2^{3x} + 1)|= 3^{2(1)} + 2^{3(1)} + 1; = 9 + 8 + 1; = 18]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Infinite Limits of Exponential Functions

Content:
Consider the graphs of [MATH: y = 2^x] and [MATH: y = 2^{-x}] shown below. We will use these graphs to compute the limits at infinity.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b74353297f24c384ed5e0930e8238b73]

Content:
Considering [MATH: y = 2^x] first, we note that as [MATH: x \to \infty,] the function increases without bound, and as [MATH: x \to -\infty,] the function approaches zero. So

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to \infty} 2^x = \infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to -\infty} 2^x =0.]

Content:
The same properties hold true for any exponential function [MATH: y=a^x] where [MATH: a \gt 1.]

Content:
Now consider the curve [MATH: y=2^{-x}.] We have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to \infty} 2^{-x} = 0\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to -\infty} 2^{-x} =\infty.]

Content:
Again, the same properties are true for any exponential function [MATH: y=a^{-x}] for [MATH: a \gt 1.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Evaluating Infinite Limits of Exponential Functions

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty} -3\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

[MATH: lim_(x → − ∞) − 3((1)/(2))^{x} = − 3 ⋅ lim_(x → − ∞)((1)/(2))^{x}]

Next, we recall the graph of [MATH: y = \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x.]

[IMG: /graphics/5846ea3956bb36f7b5955be3d8294c64]

From the graph, we see that the function increases without bound as [MATH: x] decreases. Therefore,

[MATH: \lim_{x\to-\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x = \infty.]

However, the negative factor [MATH: -3] changes the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that

[MATH: -3\cdot \lim_{x\to-\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x = -\infty.]
